intro: The design basics, explained with pins from my own library. Every principle has a way to check it, the usual mistakes, and a small study to practise it. The design-review skill uses the same names, so its notes point back here.

principles.name: One organising idea
principles.short: The site is about one thing, and everything follows from it.
principles.explain: Good sites aren't a collection of nice effects. They have one idea that decides the layout, the type, the motion and what gets left out. Obys is one centre line with a lens on it; Gionatan Nese is a slow cloud of objects. Once you have the idea, most design questions answer themselves: does this help the idea or not?
principles.check: Say the site in one sentence. Then go through every section and effect and ask whether it comes from that sentence. Anything that doesn't is decoration, and can usually go.
mistakes: Starting from a list of effects you like instead of from the subject of the site
An idea that would fit any client equally well (then it's a style, not an idea)
Adding a second big idea halfway through because the first one feels too simple
principles.practice: Take one pin you love and write its organising idea in one sentence. Then sketch the same idea for a completely different subject (a bakery, a record label, a dentist).

pins.look: One horizontal line organises the whole page: the list, the frame, the number all hang off it
No headline, no scroll: the work as small floating objects is the whole idea
Light and dark are one 3D world; the page transition pulls you through the window
What happens without an idea: generic, and the work got lost

principles.name: Design with the real content
principles.short: The real words and images shape the design, not lorem ipsum.
principles.explain: Layouts are made for content. A hero that works with a three-word name breaks with a long one; a grid made for 12 projects looks empty with 4. Designers collect the real copy, images and numbers first and design around them. The content also gives you ideas: Iva's dither effect only worked once it printed her own projects.
principles.check: Is there any placeholder text or stock image left? Count the real things (projects, products, words in the bio) and check the layout still works with the longest and the shortest one.
mistakes: Designing with lorem ipsum and finding out late that the copy doesn't fit
A layout built for 20 projects when there are 5
Writing the copy last, so it fills space instead of saying something
principles.practice: Rewrite one site's hero in three versions: 4 words, 12 words and 30 words. Lay out all three in the same grid and see which layout survives all of them.

pins.look: A copy decision changed the hero: the name moved to the nav, the hero introduces her instead
Borrow the technique, then feed it the site's own content
The work carries the page; the one line of copy only appears in the preloader
All the colour comes from the product photos, not from the interface

principles.name: One signature moment
principles.short: One thing people remember, and calm everywhere else.
principles.explain: Memorable sites usually have one moment people describe to a friend: the liquid wordmark, the cigarette that burns as you scroll, the dotted reveal. Everything around it stays quiet so it can stand out. Three signature moments on one page cancel each other out.
principles.check: What would a visitor describe to a friend afterwards? If you can't name one thing, there's no signature. If you can name four, pick one and calm down the others.
mistakes: Every section has its own big effect, so nothing stands out
The signature moment is hidden below the fold or behind a click
The moment is impressive but has nothing to do with the site's subject
principles.practice: Pick a plain one-page site you know and design only its signature moment: one interaction that comes from what the site is about. Build it as a single HTML file.

pins.look: The giant wordmark smears under the mouse; the rest of the shop is flat colour blocks
A scroll progress bar turned into a cigarette: on-brand and funny
Iva's own: her projects printed as dots, the pointer uncovers the real image
A dress-up doll as the shop's signature; one GSAP Draggable call

principles.name: Borrow the technique, not the look
principles.short: Take how something works, then make it look like this site.
principles.explain: This is the kit's manifesto. Copying a site's whole look makes yours a lesser version of it. Taking one technique (a dither, a mask, a grid that becomes a transition) and feeding it the new site's content and colours makes it yours. Never take more than one thing from one source site.
principles.check: The copy test: put your page next to the source. Would people think it's the same site? Then rework it more: new content, new form, new colours, different timing.
mistakes: Taking a site's layout, type, palette and signature motion together
Keeping the source's colours because they 'just work'
Using an effect because it's cool, without asking what it shows on this site
principles.practice: Pick one pin's technique and rebuild it with completely different content and colours. Write down what you changed and why.

pins.look: The rejected version: Aspen's dither copied as it was
The kept version: the same technique printing Iva's work
The source the technique came from

principles.name: Hierarchy
principles.short: The eye knows what to read first, second and third.
principles.explain: Every screen should have a clear order. You make it with size, weight, colour, position and space. You don't need all of them: AND2ES sets everything at 11px and makes the order with black or grey fills only; Obys makes the current project black and everything else light grey.
principles.check: The squint test: blur your eyes (or the screenshot). Can you still tell what's first, second and third? If everything has the same weight, nothing leads.
mistakes: Everything bold, big or coloured, so nothing stands out
Two things fighting to be first (a big name and a big headline)
Using five ways of emphasis at once (size + colour + caps + underline + box)
principles.practice: Set a page with one font size only and make the hierarchy with weight, fill or position. Then do the same page with size only.

pins.look: One tiny size for everything; hierarchy comes only from the black or grey fill
Current title black, the rest #c9c9c9: you read one line
Only the current page has a name; the others shrink to numbers
Two big names fought for first place; one moved to the nav

principles.name: Contrast of scale
principles.short: Very big next to very small, rarely medium.
principles.explain: Creative sites often feel designed because of extreme size jumps: a wordmark the full width of the screen above 11px body text. Medium sizes everywhere look like a template. A strong contrast also does the hierarchy for you.
principles.check: Compare your biggest and smallest type. A ratio under about 4× usually feels flat on a creative site. Count your sizes: more than 5 or 6 means the scale isn't doing its job.
mistakes: Headings only a little bigger than the body text
Lots of in-between sizes (17, 18, 20, 22, 24…)
Huge type that also shouts in colour and weight, so there's no quiet part
principles.practice: Make a poster-style page with only two sizes: one huge, one tiny. No medium allowed.

pins.look: Whisper-small body, then the wordmark the full width of the screen as the full stop
One grotesk at extreme size contrast
Huge condensed headline over small mono meta
Huge Akzidenz on a strict grid

principles.name: Space
principles.short: Empty space groups things and gives them importance.
principles.explain: Space isn't left over, it's a material. Things that are close read as a group; things far apart read as separate (that's called proximity). A small object alone in a lot of white looks precious. Most beginner layouts are too tight inside and too loose between the wrong things.
principles.check: Are related things closer to each other than to unrelated things? Is there one spacing scale (for example 4, 8, 16, 24, 48, 96) or lots of random values?
mistakes: Same spacing everywhere, so nothing groups
Filling every empty area because it 'looks unfinished'
Random margins (13px here, 22px there) instead of a scale
principles.practice: Take a busy page and remove a third of it. Use the freed space to group what's left, without adding lines or boxes.

pins.look: Small objects in a lot of white: restraint makes the work feel precious
No rules between rows; 21px rows and alignment do the grouping
An info column and one panel: two groups, nothing else

principles.name: Grid
principles.short: An invisible structure that makes the page feel intentional.
principles.explain: A grid is a set of columns (and a gutter and a margin) that everything lines up to. It's why some pages feel calm even when they're full. Once you have one, breaking it on purpose becomes a tool. Some sites even show the grid as part of the look.
principles.check: Turn on the grid overlay (G on the kit's Grids page, or the wireframe tool). Do edges line up with columns? Are breaks from the grid deliberate?
mistakes: No grid, so every section has its own widths
A grid on desktop that falls apart on the phone
Breaking the grid everywhere, so it's no longer a break
principles.practice: Lay out the same three projects on three different grids: 4 columns no gutter, 8 columns with one axis line, 12 columns asymmetric. Which one fits which mood?

pins.look: No gutters, 1px rules, content bottom-left: the grid is the look
A strict 8-column grid with one vertical rule
A visible 4-column hairline grid that also becomes the page transition
An asymmetric 12-column collage that still lines up

principles.name: Rhythm and repetition
principles.short: The same pattern repeated makes dense pages feel tidy.
principles.explain: When every project row or card follows the same pattern, a page can hold a lot without feeling messy. Repetition is also what makes a break in the pattern noticeable. GASS repeats marquee rows but gives each one a different speed, so the rhythm is alive.
principles.check: Look at a list or grid section: does every item follow the same pattern (same spacing, same caption position, same image height)? Are the exceptions on purpose?
mistakes: Every card a little different, so the page looks unplanned
Repetition with no variation anywhere, so long pages get boring
Section spacing that changes from section to section
principles.practice: Design one project row (image + caption + meta) and repeat it 10 times. Then add one deliberate variation every fourth row.

pins.look: A dense contact sheet that stays tidy because every row has the same rhythm
Every project gets the same white info card, then a mosaic
Same marquee rows, each at its own random speed

principles.name: Type voices
principles.short: One family, or a deliberate pair, each with a job.
principles.explain: Type does most of the work on a creative site. Use one family, or two (or three) faces that each have a clear job: a neutral workhorse for reading, a voice for character. Pair faces that are clearly different, not almost the same. Big type usually wants tight leading and slightly negative tracking; body text wants more air.
principles.check: How many families are on the page? Can you name each one's job? Are big headings set tighter (leading under 1, tracking slightly negative) and body text looser (leading 1.4–1.6)?
mistakes: Two faces that are almost the same (two similar grotesks)
A decorative face used for long text
Default leading and tracking on huge headings, so they look loose
principles.practice: Set the same paragraph and heading in three pairings: one family only, a grotesk + a serif at the same small size, and a neutral face + one ornate display face.

pins.look: A grotesk and a serif at the same small size, paired on one line
Three voices: a neutral grotesk, a swash script, a chunky badge face
Iva's decision: one typeface everywhere
Two faces stitched inside each letter: pairing as the signature

principles.name: Colour roles
principles.short: Few colours, each with a job, and text that reads.
principles.explain: Give each colour a role: paper (background), ink (text), accent (the one that draws the eye), mist (a quiet fill), muted (secondary text). That's how the kit's themes work. Loud palettes still work when the roles are strict: GASS uses five flat colours and rules for which text goes on which band. Text needs enough contrast to read: 4.5:1 for body text.
principles.check: List every colour on the page. Can you name each one's role? Check contrast for every text colour on every background it sits on (the specimen page and the design review do this).
mistakes: The accent used everywhere, so it no longer draws the eye
Brand colours that are too dark or too light for text on them
A different colour for every section, with no rule
principles.practice: Take one palette from a pin and write its rules: which colour is the background, which carries text, which is only for fills. Then apply those rules to a new palette.

pins.look: Five flat colours used as whole bands, with strict text rules
One bold colour carries the whole brand
Tried colour blocks, went back to white, black and one green
A brand red too dark for black text

principles.name: Restraint
principles.short: Every element has to earn its place.
principles.explain: The sites in this library that feel most expensive use very little: one or two colours, one or two faces, one effect. Restraint isn't the same as boring. It leaves room for the one thing that matters to be loud.
principles.check: Remove something (a colour, an effect, a section, a line). Is the page worse? If not, leave it out.
mistakes: Adding something every time a page feels plain
Keeping every idea because each one is nice on its own
Decoration (lines, boxes, icons) doing the job that space should do
principles.practice: Rebuild a section with half the elements: one colour, one face, no lines. Then add back only what you miss.

pins.look: Almost only the work, #fff, #000 and #e6e6e6, everything 11px
Back to white, black and one green
A small extra UI element that wasn't needed: 'Please no.'

principles.name: Motion with a job
principles.short: Every animation tells the visitor something.
principles.explain: Good motion explains: where something came from, what changed, what to look at, that the page is loading something worth waiting for. Motion without a job is just movement, and it gets tiring fast. Easing and timing matter as much as the effect: most of this kit uses an out-expo ease and durations around 0.6–1.2s.
principles.check: For each animation, finish the sentence 'this motion tells you that…'. Turn on reduced motion: does the page still work and make sense?
mistakes: Everything fades up on scroll, so motion says nothing
Animations that delay reading (long intros on every visit)
Linear or default easing, which looks mechanical
Motion that makes the content harder to see (too fast, too round, too scattered)
principles.practice: Animate the same card three ways: one that explains where it came from, one that shows it's selected, one that's only decoration. Compare how they feel.

pins.look: Hover slows the whole scene down so the busy 3D becomes readable
The layout change itself is the animation
The loading wait becomes a preview of every project
Motion that hid the work: too round, then too scattered
Stacking cards: movement with no reason for this site

principles.name: Wayfinding
principles.short: Visitors always know where they are and how to get back.
principles.explain: Creative navigation is fine as long as people don't get lost. The best pins turn navigation into a progress indicator: the list shows where you are, the nav names only the current page. Moving between pages should feel like zooming in, not like leaving.
principles.check: From any page, can you tell where you are and get back in one step? Do project pages have their own URL you can share? Does Escape close overlays, and does the back button work?
mistakes: Hiding the nav behind a clever interaction
Overlays that can't be shared or closed with Escape
Case pages with a completely different layout from the home page
principles.practice: Design a navigation that's also a progress indicator for a list of 10 projects.

pins.look: Only the current page has a name
The list is the navigation and the progress indicator
The section list scales the current name up
The case page keeps the home's centre line: arriving feels like zooming in
A drawer with its own URL, Escape closes, previous / next

principles.name: Works for everyone
principles.short: Readable, usable on a phone, with a keyboard and without motion.
principles.explain: A creative site still has to be readable and usable. That means text contrast, tap targets big enough for fingers, a version for people who turn motion off, focus outlines for keyboard users, and real text behind any WebGL. Designing the phone version early is part of the design, not a later fix.
principles.check: Look at it on a phone. Tab through it with the keyboard. Turn on reduced motion. Check contrast. The design review runs all of these.
mistakes: Hover-only interactions with no touch version
Text drawn only in a canvas, so it can't be read by screen readers or search
Light grey text on white that looks elegant but can't be read
principles.practice: Take your signature moment and design its touch version and its reduced-motion version. Both should still feel like the same idea.

pins.look: Contrast decided a colour: too dark for black text
Everything drawn in WebGL, with an sr-only copy of the text behind it
The inverting nav got hard to read over the dots

principles.name: Decide with real prototypes
principles.short: Compare working versions side by side, then choose.
principles.explain: When you can't decide, build two or three real versions and switch between them. A working prototype in the browser shows timing, scroll and feel that a static mockup hides. It's how most of Iva's decisions got made.
principles.check: Is there a decision you've been stuck on for more than a day? Build the options as switchable variants instead of thinking about it more.
mistakes: Deciding motion from a still image
Polishing one option before comparing it with the others
Throwing away the rejected versions instead of keeping them as pins
principles.practice: Build one section in two variants with a small switcher bar, and ask someone which one they'd keep and why.

pins.look: Switchable variants beat static mockups every time
Rows, Index or Strips: three work sections built to compare
Two whole versions live behind a switcher
